1:
The Hebrew says Jacob lifted up his feet, and four of them stop on the phrase because of what it implies about his spirits. Gill takes it to mean not merely that he went on foot but that he went cheerfully, the promises at Bethel having gladdened him — the Jewish writers, he adds, say his heart lifted his legs, so that he walked apace. Clarke calls the original very remarkable and hears the same cheerfulness: having seen that with God for his protector he had nothing to fear, Jacob went on his way rejoicing. Ellicott glosses it as hastening forward: confirmed in the birthright by God as well as man, and promised the divine presence and a safe return, Jacob casts no wistful glances back but travels under the inspiriting influence of hope. Calvin finds in the words the extraordinary strength of his faith, in lifting up his feet to go into a land he did not know. The country is named for its people: kedem, easterns, covering in the sacred writers all Mesopotamia and beyond the Euphrates, Clarke says, though Ellicott takes it here for the tribes of northern Mesopotamia rather than the Arabians it usually means.

Henry marks what the narrative withholds. Every stage of Israel's later march to Canaan is set down, but no journal of Jacob's expedition past Bethel — no more such nights and no more such visions, that one having been meant for a feast and not for daily bread. What he does note is the manner of the going and of the arrival. Jacob went unburdened by cares and uncramped by fears, being assured of God's presence; and after visions of God and vows made in solemn ordinances, Henry says, we should run the way of his commandments with enlarged hearts. Then providence brought him to the very field where his uncle's flocks were watered. From that his standing lesson: God is to be acknowledged in all the small circumstances that make an undertaking successful, so that if at a loss we meet someone seasonably who can direct us, or meet a disaster with help at hand, we call it neither chance nor fortune but providence — our ways are ways of pleasantness if we continually acknowledge God in them. Calvin says the same of the meeting. Jacob did not fall in with those shepherds accidentally but was guided by a hidden hand, and the men who could tell him what he needed were brought at the same hour; so whenever we wander through intricate windings we should look with the eyes of faith at the secret providence that governs us and leads us to unexpected results.

The rest of Henry's comment runs ahead into the scene at the well. The shepherds' care of their sheep illustrates the tender concern of our Lord Jesus, the great Shepherd, for his flock the church — who knows his sheep and is known of them. The stone he explains three ways: it secured a property in water that was scarce, or saved the well from the sun's heat and from any spiteful hand, or kept the lambs from drowning. That the shepherds gathered and watered together gives another maxim, that separate interests should not take men from joint help.

Two more lessons Henry draws from Jacob's manners. It becomes us to speak civilly to strangers: though a plain man dwelling in tents, Jacob addressed the men obligingly and called them brethren — the law of kindness in the tongue having commanding power. Some think he used the word because they were of his own trade, which Henry likes, a man upon his preferment not being ashamed of his trade. And those who show respect usually have it shown them: when Jacob told these strangers how to despatch their business, they did not bid him mind his own concerns but gave the reason for their delay.
2:
Gill supposes the well was sought and not stumbled on. Jacob may have looked out for one on purpose, knowing that households and shepherds come to water there and that he could ask after Laban; or he may have been looking for this particular well, where his grandfather's servant had met Rebekah, having heard of it and perhaps been directed to it. He passes on two travellers' claims — a fountain at Orpha, which is Haran, that Jews, Armenians and Turks alike called Jacob's well and the place of his service, and a fine well of excellent water near Alexandretta, not far from what the Greeks show as the ruins of Laban's house. Ellicott rules out one identification: this was not Rebekah's well, which stood just outside the city and was reached by going down steps, whereas this one lies in the open pasture. Keil and Delitzsch infer the same distance from Jacob's having to ask the men where they were from. Clarke notes that the word for the flocks means small cattle, sheep and goats, that sheep in cold countries seldom drink but the practice was probably different in a hot one, and that the three flocks already at the well were not Laban's, since his was still to come with Rachel.

What the stone was for the two of them explain differently. Clarke thinks it was made large on purpose against anyone minded to foul the water or fill the well up, which is why the first to arrive waited for the rest and they worked in concert; he adds that the rule was that it should not be shifted until every shepherd with a right to the well had come. Ellicott, rendering the clause as the stone upon the well's mouth was great, gives the dry country round Haran a practical reason — to keep the well from choking with sand — and two social ones: it restricted the water to fixed hours, needing two or three men to shift it, and it may have marked private ownership, no possession being more valued than a well. He notices who is served first. The shepherds all wait for Rachel, and her sheep drink before flocks that were there long before her, which suggests Laban held at least the first claim; no such courtesy, he remarks, was ever shown to the daughters of Jethro. Clarke reports a textual difficulty besides: where our Hebrew says all the flocks were gathered and rolled the stone away, the Samaritan reads shepherds, a reading Houbigant presses hard both here and further down, since flocks can neither roll a stone nor water sheep, and Clarke suspects the same reading stood originally in the verse before. Wesley allows the stone three uses — securing a property in water that was scarce, saving the well from the sun's heat, and keeping the lambs of the flock from drowning in it.
4:
The exchange that follows is short, and most of the comment falls on single words. Gill observes that Jacob plainly spoke to the keepers and not to the flocks. Clarke raises the question how they understood one another at all, Laban's household speaking Chaldee and not Hebrew, and answers it two ways — the names Leah afterwards gave her children show the tongues had many words in common, and Jacob may have learned Chaldee from his mother, whose native speech it was. Calvin hears in the salutation the frankness of that age: the fraternal name is often abused now by dishonest men, but friendly intercourse was then more faithfully cultivated, and Jacob greeted unknown men as brethren by received custom. The same manners, he says, explain two other things in the chapter. Rachel's tending the flock shows the frugality of the house, for Laban abounded with servants, and there is no accounting for his putting his own daughter to so vile and sordid a service except that it was then thought disgraceful to rear children in idleness, softness and indulgence — whereas now ambition and refinement have made manners so effeminate that women are for the most part ashamed of their proper office. And it was the same purity that let Jacob kiss his cousin so unceremoniously, much greater liberty being allowed in a chaste and modest way of living; in our times, Calvin adds, impurity and ungovernable lust have made not only kisses suspect but even looks dreaded, and that ancient simplicity ought to make us mourn. He also corrects the order of the narrative: Jacob did not kiss Rachel until he had told her he was her kinsman, and his weeping came partly of joy, partly of the memory of his father's house, and partly of natural affection.

Calling Laban the son of Nahor puzzles nobody for long. Gill, Clarke and Ellicott agree that son here means descendant, Laban being Bethuel's son and Nahor's grandson; Gill guesses Nahor was the better known because Haran was his city, and that Bethuel may have been dead and Laban head of the family, which is why the enquiry passes over the father to the brother. Ellicott's reason is genealogical — Nahor founded the family, being the immigrant from Ur who came to fill Abraham's place when he left.

The greeting that follows is a Hebrew idiom, and Gill and Clarke read it alike: is there peace to him, peace covering every kind of prosperity, so that the question asks after health, household and estate together. Clarke adds that Rachel's name means a ewe, and guesses she got it from her fondness for the animals.

Jacob's advice and the shepherds' refusal close the scene. Gill takes the high day for noon, when flocks in those hot countries were made to lie down by still waters, or at least for an hour with much of the day left; Clarke has the day about half run and reads Jacob as saying it is far too early to fold them, so water them and take them back to pasture. Ellicott corrects the phrase to folding the cattle and says plainly why Jacob was surprised — several hours of daylight remained — and why the men were not: if the well was Laban's, waiting for Rachel needed no explanation. As for the refusal, Gill offers either the weight of the stone, which Jarchi says took all the shepherds together, though Jacob afterwards moved it alone by his great strength, or else a custom agreed among them that it should not be opened for any one flock. Ellicott would render the answer more exactly — then they roll the stone away and we water the sheep — the removal following as soon as all the flocks are collected, each taking its turn.
9:
That a rich man's daughter should be out with the sheep strikes three of them as worth defence. Henry calls it Rachel's humility and industry — she kept her father's flock, having servants under her — and notes that her name signifies a sheep; honest useful labour, he says, is what nobody need be ashamed of, and no bar to preferment. Clarke presses further. Young women plainly were not kept shut up at home until marriage, whatever gloss is put on the word for a virgin as one concealed; nor was it beneath the greatest chief's daughters to draw water, as Rebekah did, or herd sheep, as Rachel does here. Wealth then lay in flocks, and who fitter to mind them than those with an interest in their increase? Honest labour honours high and low alike, the king himself being served by the field; there is no discredit, he concludes, in the meanest office that honestly serves the family. Ellicott brings the scene into his own century, citing Mr Malan's sight of a sheik's daughter, the beautiful and well-favoured Ladheefeh, driving her fine patriarchal sheep to a well in this very region — and does the arithmetic on Rachel: at least forty years passed between this meeting and the birth of Benjamin, so she must have been a mere child.

The stone comes off, and Clarke will not let Jacob have all the credit. Laban's flock was probably the last with a right to the well, so with its arrival the company could act; Jacob assisted the shepherds — it is not likely he did it alone — and so served a cousin who did not yet know him. Gill has the men waiting for that flock alone.

Then Jacob kisses Rachel and weeps, and the commentators sort the two acts. Gill puts the kiss after the disclosure, a courtesy once he had told her what she was to him; Ellicott gives the same order and makes the sequence the point — Jacob first made himself useful, then said who he was, claimed her as a cousin and kissed her, and only then, overcome at the happy end of a long journey and at finding himself among his own, burst into tears. In that outburst, he says, we see the beginning of his lifelong love for the beautiful child he had so opportunely met. Clarke defends the kiss as the simple and pure way the first inhabitants of the earth testified friendship, abused by hypocrites who professed affection while meditating terror, and disgraced by moralists who stumbled at innocent tokens of kindness while capable of the grossest impurity; the raised voice he takes for thanksgiving, the weeping for a sense of God's goodness and his own unworthiness. Gill notes with Aben Ezra that the telling came before both.

Henry, followed by Wesley, reads the meeting as courtship and providence together. Knowing his errand, Jacob may well have thought at once that this must be his wife, and being smitten with an honest comely face — sun-burnt, likely, and in the homely dress of a shepherdess — he is wonderfully officious to serve her. That she runs home rather than answer is to her credit, since she would not entertain a kinsman's address without her father's approbation; and such mutual respect at a first interview presaged a happy couple. What looked fortuitous was providence giving Jacob satisfaction the moment he reached the place he was bound for, as Abraham's servant had been met on a like errand — thus God guides his people with his eye. Henry also dismisses a rabbinic embellishment: it is a groundless conceit that Jacob wept because Eliphaz, Esau's eldest son, had waylaid him at his father's command and stripped him of the money and jewels his mother gave him. It was his passion for Rachel and the surprise of the meeting that drew those tears.
13:
What Laban was told, and why he ran, the three of them take differently. Gill has the report cover both the kinship and the feat — such a man at the well, so nearly allied, who had rolled the stone away and watered the flock — and notes that the Jewish writers make the message chiefly about that display of strength. Ellicott explains why the news went to the father rather than the mother's household, as Rebekah's had: this was simply the hospitable reception of a relative. To Laban it must have been welcome, calling to mind how seventy-seven years before he had watched his sister leave to marry the son of a distant sheik. One thing puzzles him: that so old a man's daughters should be so young. He offers two solutions — children of a wife of his old age, or granddaughters counted as his own because their father was dead — preferring the first, since Laban's sons go unmentioned for two chapters, probably because of their youth.

Calvin supplies the conversation the narrative omits. Laban had once seen a servant of Abraham's arrive loaded with wealth, so a poor opinion of a nephew who came with nothing might have entered his mind at once; Jacob had therefore to explain why he had left and why he was so contemptibly clothed. Probably, Calvin adds, his mother had furnished him with signs and marks by which he could prove who he was, which is why Laban's exclamation reads as a verdict: surely thou art my bone and my flesh means that he is satisfied, convinced by indubitable tokens. Gill and Clarke gloss the phrase plainly enough as nearest kin, a sister's son. Calvin turns it into a principle and widens it. Blood teaches men to help one another, but kindness ought to extend further and diffuse itself through the whole human race; and if all the sons of Adam are joined so, the spiritual relationship God creates among the faithful — than which there is no holier bond — ought to be far more effectual.

The month Ellicott renders exactly, a month of days, meaning a full one; Calvin makes it a probation. Laban did not doubt the kinship, yet tried the man's character before saying anything of wages — and the trial tells in Jacob's favour, since he did not sit idle eating another's bread for nothing but employed himself in honest labour, until Laban was obliged to admit that something beyond his keep was owing.

Laban's question about serving for nothing can be read two ways. It may mean that defrauding a relation of his wages would be grossly unjust, a kinsman deserving more consideration than a stranger; or that Laban was unwilling to exact unpaid service under colour of relationship. The second, Calvin thinks, is the better sense and received by almost everyone. What Moses means us to see is a principle of equity in Laban's own mouth — the conviction, inherent in nearly all minds, that justice should be mutually cultivated, God having engraven that law in man's nature so that whoever leaves it out of an immoderate desire for private advantage is without excuse. And then, Calvin observes, when it came to practice a little while after, Laban forgot every word of it and thought only of his own profit. Men seldom err in general principles and confess with one mouth that every man ought to have his due, yet the moment they descend to their own affairs self-love blinds them and carries them the opposite way — hence the proverb that nobody is a fit judge in his own cause. Laban's wish to settle terms is at least the right instinct, since firm compacts prevent injustice on either side: deal lawfully with your friends, the old saying runs, that you may not afterwards have to go to law with them.
15:
Laban's offer strikes most of them as fair, whatever became of it later. Henry calls the contract fair and reads Laban's reasoning approvingly: if Jacob is so respectful to his uncle as to serve for nothing, Laban will not be so unjust as to take advantage either of his necessity or of his good nature — from which Henry draws the rule that inferior relations must not be imposed on, and that if it is their duty to serve us it is ours to reward them. Wesley repeats him almost word for word. Clarke and Ellicott both suspect a motive underneath. Clarke calls Laban a very saving if not covetous man who had watched a month's work and meant to secure so useful a servant; Ellicott, noting that Jacob had already given a full account of himself on arrival, thinks Laban probably expected the very answer he got — though he grants the proposal was fair and upright, a month having shown how valuable the services would be.

Henry also praises what Jacob did with that month. He was not idle, nor spent his time in sport and pastime, but like a man of business, with no stock of his own, applied himself to serve his uncle as he had begun at the well; wherever we are, Henry says, it is good to be employed in some useful business that will turn to good account.

The two sisters are then set side by side, and the comparison turns on a single word. Gill takes tender-eyed for blear-eyed, a moisture that reddened them and made her less agreeable to look at, though Onkelos, he records, rendered it the other way, as if her beauty lay in her eyes and nowhere else. Ellicott agrees with the unflattering sense — Leah, whose name means languor or weariness, had dull bleared eyes, probably from some form of ophthalmia, common enough in that hot sandy region — and observes that in the East such eyes counted a great defect where bright ones were much admired. Clarke dissents. The Hebrew, he says, means soft, delicate, lovely, the reverse of the sense usually given it: the writer is comparing the sisters, and the balance still falls to Rachel, beautiful in shape, person, mien and gait and beautiful in countenance, so that Leah's chief recommendation was precisely her soft and beautiful eyes. Ellicott ends where neither of the others goes: it was not Rachel, with her fair face and her husband's lasting love, who became mother of the Messiah's progenitor, but the weary-eyed Leah.

Why Jacob offered service rather than money Clarke explains from the custom. In his destitute state he could produce no dowry, and in those times it was the father who received a portion for his daughter and not the father who gave one with her; he quotes a Hindoo lawgiver to the effect that a person may become a slave on account of love, or to obtain a wife. He then turns it into a complaint about his own age: the bad system of education by which women are spoiled and rendered generally good for nothing makes it necessary now for a husband to get a dowry to maintain her, whereas formerly they were well educated and extremely useful, so that a man who got a wife almost invariably got a prize — or, as Solomon says, a good thing.

Henry does the arithmetic and finds it startling. Jacob was seventy-seven years old, by his reckoning, when he bound himself apprentice for a wife and kept sheep for a wife — a thing his posterity are reminded of long afterwards as a mark of the meanness of their origin. Wesley makes the figure seventy. Both suppose Rachel was young and scarcely marriageable when Jacob came, which made him the readier to wait out the seven years for her.
18:
Gill dates the love from the well: Jacob loved Rachel from the moment he saw her, finding her beautiful, modest, humble, affable, diligent and industrious. Ellicott attends to how she is named — the Hebrew calls her the little one, as Leah is the great one, the phrase meaning simply the younger — and explains the shape of the offer. Wives had to be purchased in the East, and Jacob, having brought none of the rich presents Abraham once sent when seeking a wife for his son, had nothing to offer but his own service. He adds a consequence to watch for: since such a sale was ordinarily veiled, in true Oriental fashion, under the specious form of freewill gifts, both daughters will afterwards be found offended at being so openly bartered.

Calvin will not have the transaction called anything but what it was. It is a shameful barbarity, he says, to hand over a daughter as the reward of service and make her the subject of a kind of barter; Laban should have assigned her a portion and dealt more liberally with his son-in-law, and instead, under the pretext of kinship, defrauded him of the wages of his labour — the very injustice he had himself named a moment before. Nor is Moses recording anything rare: men do not put their daughters up for sale, but the desire of gain hurries most of them far enough to prostitute their honour and sell their souls.

On Jacob's preference Calvin is careful rather than censorious. That he inclined to Rachel is no fault in itself, since a secret affection naturally produces mutual love, and a man drawn to a wife by elegance of form does not necessarily sin, provided reason keeps the ascendancy and holds the wantonness of passion under. Only excess must be guarded against, the more diligently because such affections are hard to keep from stifling reason. Yet Calvin suspects some self-indulgence — asking the younger sister to the injury of the elder and, yielding to the desire of his eyes, undervaluing what Leah had, when excellence of disposition ought to weigh first and choosing for beauty alone is a very culpable want of self-government. What he praises without qualification is the seven years: the strength and ardour of the attachment showed in a man who felt no weariness in that labour, and chastity was joined with it, so that he persevered with a patient and quiet mind through the whole of it. Here again the integrity and continence of that age appears — living under one roof in daily familiar intercourse, Jacob conducted himself with modesty and abstained from every impropriety, which is why he could say at the end, give me my wife that I may go in unto her, implying she had till then been a pure virgin.

Laban's answer Gill will not take at face value. He agrees with the Targum of Jonathan that it was spoken deceitfully, a pretence of great respect from a man who already meant to impose upon him. Ellicott, on the other hand, finds the reply entirely in keeping with the custom of the country. Arabs still prefer a relative as husband for a daughter, and on payment of a moderate dowry the elder cousins may claim the elder daughters and the younger the younger — so that Jacob, as a second son, had a claim upon Rachel. He reports the rabbinic notion that Leah's eyes were weak from weeping because Esau had never come to marry her, and though he calls it absurd he thinks it good evidence that cousin-marriage was an established rule, and reason enough for Laban to accept Jacob for his younger child. That Jacob offered seven years for Rachel, and afterwards gave a second seven for her when he had been tricked into Leah, suggests to him that the term was not thought unreasonable.
20:
Gill says only that Jacob served the whole term, diligently, faithfully and patiently. Clarke turns the seven years into a survey of how wives were got. In ancient times it was the custom among all nations for men to give dowries for their wives, and in many countries it still is: Shechem offered whatever was asked for Dinah, Eliezer carried a profusion of silver, gold, jewels and raiment for Rebekah, David had to kill Goliath and then a hundred Philistines before he was allowed Michal, and Hosea bought his wife for fifteen pieces of silver and a homer and a half of barley. The same custom held among the ancient Greeks, Indians and Germans; the Romans had a form of marriage by purchase; the Tartars and the Turks still buy their wives, and among the latter as a sort of slaves.

Then the strangest parallel he can find, from Herodotus on the Babylonians. Every district assembled its marriageable virgins once a year, and the crier sold them one by one, always bringing forward the most beautiful first; the richest contended and outbid one another for the fairest, while the common sort took the ugly and the lame with money — for when the beautiful were gone the crier put up the most deformed and asked who would marry her for the smallest sum. So the price of the handsome made the portion of those whose look was disagreeable or who had some bodily imperfection. A father might not indulge his own fancy in choosing a husband, and no purchaser could carry off the woman he had bought without giving security that he would live with her as his wife; those who took money with a bride who could fetch no price gave the same security, and had to refund if they failed. Laban, Clarke concludes, used Rachel's beauty to dispose of Leah in the spirit of that custom, though not in the letter.

The clause about the seven years seeming a few days raises a difficulty Clarke cannot leave alone. If Jacob really waited the whole term before marrying, could the time possibly be said to have seemed short? Some eminent men, he reports, have contended that he received Rachel soon after the first month and then served his seven years for her, which might truly feel like a few days as his love increased; others think that irreconcilable with the circumstances, and suppose instead that Jacob was not seventy-seven at this point but fifty-seven, which leaves room enough for everything the history records of his stay. As for the incredibility of a lover waiting seven years and calling them short, Clarke answers it twice over: he had the continual company of his chosen bride, which takes the tedium out of any delay, and love affairs among the patriarchs were never carried to the pitch of insanity they reach in modern times — those men were sober and sedate, scarcely married before forty, and married then more for convenience and the desire of offspring than for anything else. At the lowest computation Jacob had long passed the age when passion runs away with reason. Still, Clarke admits, the obvious construction of the text is that he got Rachel the week after he married Leah.

Ellicott reckons the age at fifty-seven at least, and explains it by the late marriages of the patriarchs generally, who seem to have arrived at manhood only slowly; on that footing the warmth of Jacob's affection needs no apology, and it was no passing emotion but lasted his whole life. He marks the verse as a turning point too — this is the last of the late marriages, since Jacob's own sons married young. Wesley takes the phrase somewhere else entirely: an age of work, he says, will be but a few days to those that love God and long for Christ's appearing.
21:
Jacob's demand is a claim of right, and all three read it so. Gill has him challenge Rachel as his wife already, hers by contract, the conditions performed; Clarke puts it plainly — the seven years are complete, let me have the wife for whom I have given this service as a dowry; Ellicott glosses the phrase as the appointed term being finished, and concludes flatly that the marriage took place at the end of the seven years.

The feast that follows Gill takes for a public act. Laban gathered the men of Haran, or at least its chief and principal men, to make his daughter's marriage open and authentic. Clarke reads the word for the feast as one of drinking: marriage being a very solemn contract, there is much reason to think sacrifices were offered and libations poured out, and since a cup of wine was handed to every guest and drunk with particular ceremonies, the meal may have taken its name from the most prominent thing about it. Calvin restrains the scale — not a supper for the whole town but many guests invited, as at any splendid wedding — and finds a motive in the splendour. Laban took the more trouble over the feast in order to bind Jacob by shame, so that he should not afterwards dare to make light of the marriage he had been tricked into. From the same verse Calvin draws an observation about the customs of the marriage bed, and the deception turns on it: out of regard for the modesty of brides they were led veiled into the chamber. That ancient discipline being now thrown off, he adds, men have become almost brutal.

How the substitution succeeded the three explain the same way. Gill sets it after the feast, the guests gone and night fallen, a fit season for such a design. Clarke lists the conditions: the bride always veiled, the bride-chamber generally dark or nearly so, and Leah brought in at evening — so the imposition might easily pass undetected until the next day discovered it. Ellicott adds that the bride was carried closely veiled to the bridegroom's house and that there was probably some similarity of voice and figure between the sisters, then draws a conclusion the others do not: Leah must have been party to the fraud, so that Jacob's later dislike of her was not altogether without reason.

Keil and Delitzsch look ahead to the excuse Laban would make in the morning, and refuse it outright. He pleaded the custom of the place, that the younger is not given before the first-born; but the plea is perfectly worthless, since if such a custom really held in Haran, as it has held in ancient India and elsewhere, he was bound to have told Jacob of it beforehand. What he offered instead was the younger daughter in a week's time, at the price of another seven years' service.

The handmaid given with Leah closes the scene, and the comment is all about how little it was. Gill observes that it was usual to give several at such a time, as Rebekah seems to have had, whereas Leah had one, and that one was the whole portion Jacob got with her; he reports the Targum of Jonathan's claim that Zilpah was Laban's own daughter by a concubine, and the Jewish saying which follows from it, that a man's daughters by his concubines are called maids. Clarke notes the legal point, that slaves given to a daughter at her marriage were her peculiar property, over whom the husband had neither right nor power. Ellicott sharpens the comparison: Bethuel had given Rebekah her nurse Deborah and damsels besides, but she had been bought with presents of unusual costliness — and Laban does not seem to have dealt liberally by his daughters, who resented his treatment of them long afterwards.
25:
Morning ends it, and Gill wonders how the night had not. Daylight and the lifted veil showed the tender eyes; it is much, he says, that her voice had not betrayed her, unless the sisters sounded alike or she kept silence. Excusing her he finds hard — the sin is adultery and incest — though he assembles what can be said. She obeyed her father; being eldest she may have wished a husband first, and above all the promised seed, which was to run in Jacob's line; and Schmidt suggests Laban had persuaded her the contract was made on her account. The same said to Rachel, Gill adds, would account for her acquiescing, otherwise hard to explain.

Wesley states the retribution in a sentence: Jacob had cheated his own father by pretending to be Esau, and now his father-in-law cheated him — and however unrighteous Laban was, the Lord was righteous in it. Calvin thinks Jacob's expostulation justified and Laban's answer no excuse, though he grants it a pretext. It was not the custom to marry the younger first, and the first-born would have been wronged by disturbing that order; but Laban should have said so in time, and turned Jacob's thoughts toward Leah or warned him off both. From this Calvin draws the shape of the whole man: once deceitful men have turned aside from truth they make no end of transgressing, and always keep some pretext by them to clear themselves of blame. He counts the offences — demanding seven years' labour for a daughter, selling her without a dowry for gain, and worst of all robbing his nephew of his betrothed wife, perverting the laws of marriage and leaving nothing safe or sound — and observes that the man still contrived to look as if he had an honourable defence.

Whether the custom existed at all divides the rest. Gill takes Laban at his word, noting that he denies neither the deceit nor the agreement but pleads the usage of the city against both. Clarke thinks the rule genuine and old: daughters were early given in marriage by seniority, and the Hindoos, the oldest people now existing next to the Jews, hold this not as custom but as positive law, counting it an offence equal to adultery for a man to marry while an elder brother is unmarried, or for a father to give a younger daughter while the eldest remains single — Laban's words, he says, are literally what a Hindoo would say. What Clarke holds against him is the concealment, the custom kept back until Leah had been delivered. Ellicott is more sceptical. The practice is such as Laban describes in India, but there is no proof of it among the Bedaween; and since Leah apparently loved Jacob and Laban wanted his service continued, he suspects an unscrupulous plot between the two of them on a pretext overstrained if not false. Jacob plainly knew of no such rule, and would never have given seven years for Leah. Wesley says the same more shortly: we have reason to think there was no such custom, and if there was, Laban should have said so when he took seven years' service for the younger daughter.

Keil and Delitzsch look past the excuse to what it produced, refusing both ways of settling it. Let Leah's marriage-week pass over, they render it; the feast generally ran a week, and when it ended Jacob received the younger too — two wives in eight days, one maid apiece, less than Bethuel gave his own daughter. The bigamy that followed, they insist, is not to be judged by a Mosaic law against marrying two sisters that did not yet exist, nor set down as incest, as Calvin sets it down; but neither is it justified on the ground that God's blessing afterwards made it the means of multiplying Abraham's seed into a nation.
27:
Whose week is meant nearly everyone settles the same way. Gill takes it for Leah's, the seven days of marriage feasting and not a week of years, citing the Jewish writers and the Targum of Jerusalem; Ellicott and Clarke agree the festival ran a week, as later. Clarke adds the practical reason Laban could not hand Rachel over at once: the solemnities had begun before all the men of the place, it would not have done to break them off, and probably he wanted the fraud kept out of the public eye. Ellicott puts it in terms of honour — to forsake Leah during those days would have been an insult her brothers must have avenged — so Jacob, appeased by the promise of Rachel at the week's end and unwilling to quarrel with the household, submitted to the wrong. He notes the Hebrew is remarkable — fulfil the week of this, and we will give thee also the this for the service — and insists the idiom means the one and the other, so the first can only be Leah and the second only Rachel. Calvin alone refers the demonstrative to Rachel and reads the verse as the purchase of marriage with her by a second seven years — not that Laban put off the wedding to the term's end, but that Jacob was bound into a fresh servitude.

What it cost Clarke reckons plainly: fourteen years' service instead of seven, since Jacob would hardly have served seven days for Leah with his affection set wholly on Rachel, and by the stratagem Laban got both daughters settled. What a man sows he reaps — Jacob had practised deceit and is now deceived, and Laban, the instrument, was deceived himself after. Wesley reads it as a snare rather than a bargain. Jacob had no design of multiplying wives and would have kept as true to Rachel as his father to Rebekah, having lived without a wife to his eighty-fourth year and been content with one; it was Laban, wanting to dispose of two daughters without portions and get seven more years of labour, who forced him into a strait where he had colourable reason for marrying both.

Calvin is harshest, and calls the man callous in wickedness. Had Laban owned ten more daughters he would have disposed of them the same way, obtruding his child as merchandise and thinking nothing of the disgrace so long as it turned a profit. The graver charge is what it did to the household: he involved his nephew in polygamy and polluted him and his own daughters with incestuous nuptials, setting two sisters in one bed so that each became the other's competitor and they spent their lives in hostility. Better to repudiate an unloved wife, Calvin argues, than keep her captive and let a second consume her with grief — which is why the Lord by Malachi pronounces divorce more tolerable than polygamy. That such licence was common among oriental nations he grants; it did not entitle men to overturn by a depraved custom the law of marriage sanctioned from the beginning. And since Moses sets these crimes at the opening of Israel's history, its people have no business boasting of holy fathers, for however excellent Jacob was, his offspring sprang from an impure source — two sisters mixed in one marriage, two concubines added after.

Nor does Calvin let Jacob off. Necessity may excuse him in part but cannot absolve him: he might have dismissed Leah, who had never been his lawful wife, marriage being constituted by the mutual consent of the man and the woman, about which no mistake is possible. Instead he reluctantly kept a woman he was free of, doubling his fault by polygamy and trebling it by an incestuous marriage — proof, Calvin thinks, that his love for Rachel burned until he had neither moderation nor judgment left.
28:
Whether Jacob is to be blamed for the double marriage is the question, and no two answer it alike. Clarke acquits him. It is perfectly plain, he says, that Jacob did not serve another seven years before getting Rachel — he kept the week with Leah and the feast, then received her and served the second term after; such connections are now called incestuous but were allowable then, and no blame appears to attach to him, though the women's jealousies vexed him ever after. Clarke even makes the case the origin of a later statute: it was probably on this account that the law forbade taking a wife to her sister to vex her in her lifetime.

Gill leaves the justification open. Marrying two sisters was forbidden by the law of Moses and polygamy disallowed later, yet both were dispensed with earlier; and he sees an overruling providence, which brings good out of evil, since the Messiah was to spring from Leah and not Rachel, the plurality of wives seeming permitted so that Jacob might have his promised progeny. He also pleads necessity: one sister had been ignorantly defiled by him and the other was his by contract, and he could not have her except by marrying the other, keeping her week and serving seven years more.

Ellicott asks outright: after the monogamy of Abraham and the stricter monogamy of Isaac, how came Jacob to have two wives? He reports Abravanel's answer, that since Esau ought to have married Leah and Jacob Rachel, Jacob acted only as his brother's substitute in taking the elder and stayed free to marry the younger, who was his by custom; and that remembering the promise of a seed numerous as the dust, and how near the family had come to extinction, he wished to secure it. Ellicott's own view is simpler: even after Leah was forced on him Jacob regarded Rachel as his own, and polygamy not being forbidden he thought he did no more than justice to her and himself — Esau having been blamed not for two wives but for taking Hittites, and a man in love needing little argument. The only alternative, divorcing Leah, would have been worse — and divorce was not yet a practice.

Keil and Delitzsch call it sinful weakness but not what Calvin calls it. Jacob's fault showed itself in loving Rachel more than Leah, and God's chastisement in the hated wife's being blessed with children while Rachel long remained unfruitful — by which it appeared once more that the origin of Israel was a work not of nature but of grace.

Calvin takes the whole episode as a warning against the habit of looking to the fathers. Moses meant to exhibit Jacob's sins so that we might learn to fear and square every action by the sole rule of God's word; if so holy a patriarch fell this grievously, none of us is safe except as God keeps him. It shows how dangerous it is to imitate the fathers while neglecting the law of the Lord — and yet the foolish Papists will observe as law whatever they find the fathers to have done, owning as fathers men worthy of such sons. Nor is Leah spared: she was not despised without fault of her own, and the Lord justly chastised her, since knowing her father's fraud she dishonourably took her sister's husband; but her fault, Calvin ends, is no excuse for Jacob's lust. Gill adds that Rachel too was given a handmaid, whom the Targum of Jonathan likewise makes Laban's daughter by a concubine.
31:
One word governs the verse, and how far to soften it is the question. Gill takes hated comparatively: Jacob did a husband's duty to Leah, so she was loved less rather than hated — and much can be said for it, since she had not Rachel's beauty, was never his choice, was imposed on him by deceit, and had to be married if he was to have Rachel. Clarke turns this into a rule of interpretation that he thinks settles some disputed passages. To hate, in the idiom, means simply to love less; Jacob's frequent company with Leah proves he did not hate her as we use the word, but showed her less affection than her sister. On that footing he reads the saying that Jacob was loved and Esau hated as meaning only a greater degree of affection shown to one family than the other, in giving it a better earthly portion and choosing it for the Messiah's line — not one word of it, he insists, touching the eternal state of either nation. Those who prop up the peculiarities of their creed with such texts, he ends, greatly err, knowing neither the Scripture nor the mercy of God.

Ellicott refuses the softening: we must not tone it down too much, for plainly Leah was not the object of love at all; it was her fruitfulness that gave her value in her husband's eyes, and when that ceased he neglected her utterly. Calvin steers between the two and makes the word a charge against Jacob rather than a description of his feelings. Leah was not intolerable to him, nor pursued with hatred; Moses chooses so hard a word to amplify the fault of a man who did not discharge a husband's duty or treat his first wife with the honour due to her. Calvin presses the distinction, because many suppose they have done their duty if they stop short of mortal hatred — whereas the Holy Spirit pronounces those hated who are not sufficiently loved. None will be held guiltless of hatred but he who embraces his neighbours with love; not open displeasure only, but the neglect of brethren and the cold charity that reigns in the world. The closer the tie the stronger the bond, so that married people who never openly disagree may still be guilty, a coldness between them being not far from hating.

Calvin also reads the birth as a correction. Jacob's extravagant love was tamed by the rod, as the affections of the faithful are when they grow inordinate; Rachel was loved to her sister's wrong, and the Lord stepped in as Leah's vindicator, turning her husband's mind toward the quarter it had been most averse to. From that he takes two lessons: that offspring is a special gift of God, the power of making one woman fruitful and cursing another's womb being ascribed to him, and that children conciliate husbands to wives.

Henry and Wesley read the same providence as a balancing of accounts. Leah, the less beloved, is blessed with children while Rachel is denied them — and see, Henry says, how Providence keeps the scale even, setting crosses and comforts one against another so that nobody is too much elevated or too much cast down. Rachel wants children and has her husband's love; Leah wants the love and is fruitful, as between Elkana's two wives; for the Lord is wise and righteous. The child was three things at once: a rebuke to Jacob for making so great a difference between women he was equally related to, a check to Rachel, who had perhaps insulted her sister over it, and a comfort to Leah, that she should not be overwhelmed by the contempt put on her. Wesley adds the comparison that makes the hard word bearable: in this sense a man is required to hate father and mother in comparison with Christ.
32:
Every one of the four names is a sentence, and they are read as Leah's running commentary on her own life. Reuben Clarke renders literally, behold a son, because Jehovah had looked on her affliction; Keil and Delitzsch say the names indicate her state of mind throughout, this first taken as a pledge that the Lord had regarded her misery, so that now her husband would love her. Gill hesitates between two derivations — see the son, as if she were calling husband and household to come and look, or rather God has seen and provided a son, which he thinks fits the rest of the verse better. He allows a guess about her hopes and then corrects it: she may have imagined this was the promised seed to come of Abraham in Jacob's line, but if so she was greatly mistaken, for this son proved unstable and did not excel.

Calvin makes the naming an act of gratitude and infers a habit of prayer behind it. Leah was not ungrateful, and God's benefits were better appreciated in that age than in his own, when a profane stupor so occupies nearly all men that, like cattle, they swallow whatever kindness God bestows. She does not merely own him as author of her fruitfulness; she gives a reason, that her affliction had been looked on and a son granted who should draw her husband's affection to her. Whence it seems likely, Calvin argues, that when she found herself despised she had recourse to prayer — thanksgiving being proof of prayer beforehand, since those who hope for nothing from God bury his favours in forgetfulness. So she wrote a memorial on her child to stir herself up to praise. The verse teaches besides that those unjustly despised by men are regarded by the Lord, a singularly profitable consolation to the faithful, who are mostly despised in the world: when treated harshly, let them take refuge in the thought that God will be the more propitious.

The other three names Calvin runs through the same way. The second she took from hearing, to keep in memory that her sighs had been heard, from which he concludes she had cast her griefs into God's bosom while the affliction pressed; the third from joining, as if to say a new link was interposed and she must now be better loved; and in the fourth she declares her piety again by naming him praise. She had given thanks already, Calvin observes, but with more abundant matter for praise supplied she acknowledges God's help not once, and not by a single method, but again and again.

Wesley reads the same series as the record of a marriage. Leah appears very ambitious of her husband's love and reckoned the want of it her affliction — not upbraiding him with it as his fault, but laying it to heart as her grief, which she had the more reason to bear because she had consented to the fraud by which she became his wife. So she called her first-born see a son, with the pleasant thought that now her husband would love her, and her third joined, in the expectation that now he would be joined to her; and when she said the Lord had heard, she meant that he had taken notice she was hated. Her fourth she called praise, saying, now will I praise the Lord — and this, Wesley adds, was he of whom, as concerning the flesh, Christ came. Whatever is the matter of our rejoicing ought to be the matter of our thanksgiving, and all our praises must centre in Christ, as their matter and Mediator both, since he descended from one whose very name was praise. Gill remarks only that the births came as fast as they well could, and reports the Jewish notion that Leah brought forth her sons at seven months.
34:
The third name Clarke reads as a calculation. Levi means joined, and he supposes Leah reckoned that after so many children Jacob would be bound to her in affection at least as strong as he bore Rachel; he then notices where the name led, since from this son sprang the Levites, who instead of the first-born were joined to the priests in the service of the sanctuary.

The fourth gathers up the rest, and Gill dwells on it because of what came out of it. This was a son in whose line and from whose tribe the Messiah was to spring, and Leah, who had praised God already for looking on her affliction, for hearing her, and for one child after another, now determines to praise him more than ever. Gill passes on the Targum of Jonathan's reason for the name — that from this son should come kings, and David the king, who should praise the Lord — and asks why she may not as well be supposed to have known that the Messiah would spring from him, which would greatly heighten her joy. He adds, from the Jewish writers, a calendar of the four births and the ages the sons reached.

Clarke renders the name a confessor, one who acknowledges God and that every good thing comes out of his hand, and gives him the praise due to his grace and mercy. From this patriarch, he observes, the Jews take their name — and if it could now be rightly applied, it would mean a people that confess God, own his bounty and praise him for his grace.

On the closing words Clarke corrects the English. She stood still from bearing is what the Hebrew says, which is not what left bearing conveys: the one sounds as if she ceased entirely, whereas she had several children afterwards, and the pause was probably caused by a temporary suspension of Jacob's company through Rachel's jealous management. He ends the chapter with a complaint about naming in his own day. The care of the world's first inhabitants to call their children after some remarkable providence, or circumstance of their birth, deserves not respect only but imitation, since a name that keeps recalling the occasion to parents and child alike cannot fail to be a lasting blessing. How widely different is our custom: unthinking and ungodly, we impose names on our offspring as we do on our cattle, so that the dog, the horse, the monkey and the parrot share in common with our children the names that pass for Christian — some of them absurd, others ridiculous, and a third sort downright impious, being taken from the demon gods and goddesses of heathenism. Clarke closes with a hope that the rational and pious custom the Scriptures recommend may one day be restored, even among those who profess to believe in, fear and love God.
